result:
**Recommendation: REST** (JSON over HTTP, described with OpenAPI) for a new public API, unless your consumers are mostly front-end teams building rich, highly varied UIs on top of a deeply connected data graph.

| Factor | REST | GraphQL |
|---|---|---|
| Consumer onboarding | Universal: curl, any HTTP client, any language | Requires a GraphQL client and learning the query language |
| Caching | HTTP caching, CDNs and ETags work out of the box | Mostly POST to one endpoint; needs persisted queries or client-side caching |
| Rate limiting and abuse control | Simple per-endpoint limits | Needs query cost analysis, depth limits and complexity budgets |
| Fetch flexibility | Fixed shapes; can over-fetch or need several round trips | Client asks for exactly what it needs in one request |
| Evolution | Explicit versioning, which is clunky but well understood | Additive schema plus field deprecation, with no versions |
| Typing and tooling | OpenAPI gives SDK generation, docs and mocking | Strong built-in schema, introspection and excellent tooling |
| Performance predictability | Each endpoint has a known cost | Arbitrary queries; N+1 and expensive joins are your problem |
| Error handling and observability | HTTP status codes, standard logs and metrics per route | Often 200 with errors in the body; needs per-field tracing |

**Why REST wins for a public API**
- **You don't control the clients.** With GraphQL, anonymous third parties can compose arbitrarily expensive queries, and defending against that is ongoing work.
- **The barrier to entry is lower.** Public API adoption depends on someone getting a successful call in five minutes, and nearly every developer already knows REST.
- **The operational surface is simpler.** Caching, rate limiting, monitoring, gateways and WAFs all understand REST natively.
- **Stable contracts are easier to guarantee.** A fixed set of endpoints is easier to document, test and give SLAs for.

**When to pick GraphQL instead**
- Your data is a deep graph and consumers need very different slices of it, as with the GitHub and Shopify APIs.
- The main consumers are mobile or web apps where round trips and payload size matter.
- You have the capacity to build query cost limiting, persisted queries and dataloader-style batching from the start.

**Getting most of GraphQL's benefits with REST**
- Add sparse fieldsets (`?fields=id,name`) and expansion (`?expand=customer`) to cut over-fetching and round trips.
- Use cursor-based pagination and consistent filtering conventions.
- Write the OpenAPI spec first and generate SDKs and docs from it.

If you later find a real need for flexible querying, you can add a GraphQL layer on top of the REST services; going the other way is harder.

If you tell me who the consumers are and what the data model looks like, I can check whether this default holds for your case.
